Claude Elwood Shannon (1916–2001) was an American mathematician, electrical engineer, and cryptographer, widely recognized as the 'father of information theory.' His landmark 1948 paper, 'A Mathematical Theory of Communication,' established the foundational concepts for the digital age, including the bit, entropy, and the limits of data compression and transmission.

In his 1937 master's thesis, Shannon proved that Boolean algebra could be used to optimize the design of systems of electromechanical relays used in telephone routing switches. This insight effectively laid the theoretical groundwork for all modern digital computer design by demonstrating that electronic circuits could implement logic functions.

Beyond information theory and digital logic, Shannon made significant contributions to artificial intelligence, cryptography, and game theory. He designed 'Theseus,' a robotic mouse capable of navigating a maze, and authored seminal papers on computer chess, including an estimate for the game's complexity. During World War II, he worked at Bell Labs on cryptography and fire-control systems.

Shannon spent much of his career at MIT and Bell Labs. Known for his eclectic interests, he was also an avid inventor and hobbyist, creating devices such as rocket-powered frisbees and juggling robots. His work remains central to the fields of telecommunications, computing, and signal processing.
